title: Walls and Gates
statement: You are given an m x n grid of rooms. -1 is a wall, 0 is a gate, and 2147483647 (treat it as INF) is an empty room. Fill each empty room with the number of steps to its nearest gate, moving only up, down, left or right and never through a wall. If a room cannot reach any gate, leave it as INF. Modify the grid in place.
realWorld: Nearest-facility labelling on a floor plan or mesh: marking every square metre of a warehouse with the walking distance to the closest exit, charging dock or fire escape. The same computation produces a latency map from several points of presence, where each cell takes the distance to whichever POP is nearest.

examples.input: rooms = [[INF,-1,0,INF],[INF,INF,INF,-1],[INF,-1,INF,-1],[0,-1,INF,INF]]  (rows of a matrix; INF is 2147483647)
examples.explanation: Two gates, at (0,2) and (3,0). Every room takes the smaller of its two distances — (1,0) is 2 steps from the bottom-left gate and 4 from the top gate, so it holds 2.
A gate at each end. The two middle rooms are each 1 step from the nearer gate, not 1 and 2 from the left one — which is the whole point of seeding both gates at once.
The bottom-right room is walled off. Unreachable rooms keep INF; they are not 0 and not -1.

bruteForce.idea: Run a separate BFS from each gate, and for every room keep the smallest distance any of those searches produced.
code: int[][] distance = bfsFrom(rooms, r, c);      // a full sweep of the grid, per gate

complexity.space: O(m * n) for each distance grid

bruteForce.whySlow: Every gate walks the entire reachable grid, and almost all of that walking is thrown away by the Math.min. A room three steps from the nearest gate is still visited by every far gate, each of which computes a larger number that loses the comparison. On a 250x250 grid where a tenth of the cells are gates, the same 62,500 cells are traversed 6,000 times over to produce one number per cell — the comparison work is real, but the traversal work behind it was decided before it started.

patternIdentification: The answer at each room is a minimum over many starting points. BFS already reaches nodes in increasing order of distance, so if all the starting points sit in the queue together at distance 0, the frontier expands as one wave and the first time it touches a room, it has arrived from the nearest source. The minimum is taken by the ordering, for free, instead of by comparison afterwards. Multi-source BFS is the general move: whenever a problem says 'nearest' or 'earliest' over a set of origins, seed every origin at level 0 rather than running one search per origin. This is the same technique as rotting-oranges, where every rotten orange is a source and each BFS level is one minute.

optimized.idea: Scan once to push every gate into the queue. Then run a single BFS. Because a room is only written when its value is still INF, the first arrival wins and later, longer arrivals are rejected by the same test that serves as the visited check — the grid itself is the visited set. Each cell is enqueued at most once, so the whole thing is one linear pass over the grid regardless of how many gates there are.
code: if (rooms[r][c] == 0) queue.offer(new int[]{r, c});   // EVERY gate is a level-0 source
int r = cell[0] + d[0], c = cell[1] + d[1];
if (r < 0 || r >= rows || c < 0 || c >= cols) continue;
if (rooms[r][c] != INF) continue;      // wall, gate, or already reached by a nearer gate

complexity.space: O(m * n) for the queue in the worst case

visualization.title: Multi-source BFS: every gate seeded at distance 0, so first arrival is nearest gate

commonMistakes: Running one BFS per gate and taking the minimum — the answers are correct but a 250x250 grid dense with gates does thousands of full sweeps and times out, which reads like a wrong algorithm rather than a wrong seeding.

Guarding the neighbour with rooms[r][c] != -1 instead of rooms[r][c] == INF — gates (value 0) then pass the test, get overwritten with a distance, get re-enqueued, and the two gates keep re-flooding each other; the method never terminates.

Pre-filling the grid with 0 or -1 instead of leaving unreachable rooms at INF — the walled-off room in example 3 comes back as 0, which reads as 'there is a gate here' and is the worst possible wrong answer for a nearest-exit map.
